Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-30 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Elena (Redwood SE), Connor (Redwood SE), Maya (Stratus Orbit CTO), Liam (Platform), Aria (Product), Raj (Security)
Recording: (internal link)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to decide between PLG/self-serve hosted flow vs reserved/dedicated pilot; primary concerns: data residency, SSO/KMS, time-to-first-token, and how the free credits/quickstart map to a pilot.

Topics: onboarding path, credits, VPC/private deployment considerations, latency vs cost tradeoffs, SOC2/KMS, pilot success criteria.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro, I'm Samir, AE at Redwood, with Elena and Connor on the engineering side. how's everyone doing?
[00:12] Maya: Good, thanks. we're excited — trying to figure out how fast we can get something internal running.
[00:18] Liam: Yeah our timelines are tight. we have a roadmap item to ship a first internal assistant for support by end of Q4 so..
[00:26] Samir: Perfect. high level goal today: figure out whether you can go PLG/self-serve hosted to validate, or if you need a reserved/dedicated or private deployment from day one. we can also discuss the free credits and typical time-to-first-token.
[00:40] Aria: The main questions for product — latency matters for UX, and security/residency matters for data classification.
[00:47] Elena: Great, can you walk me through your infra? are you cloud-first, any requirements for VPC peering or on-prem?
[00:55] Maya: We run in GCP, internal customer data is marked PII. For initial experiments it's fine to use hosted if data doesn't leave region, but for pilot we might need VPC or private deployment.
[01:08] Raj: Also SOC2 and encryption at rest, KMS integration — if we move to dedicated we need to ensure customer-managed keys.
[01:16] Samir: Totally. Redwood hosted supports region controls and SOC2 compliant handling; for KMS we have integrations and private deployments support customer-managed keys and HSMs. Elena will share the security pack.
[01:28] Speaker 1: (mumble) how about latency numbers?
[01:31] Elena: Good question. depends on model and sequence length, but for typical 256-token chat we see p50 latencies in our hosted environment around 60–120ms per token with optimized models; end-to-end response times often 300–800ms depending on prompt size and streaming. if you need sub-200ms total we can look at dedicated nodes in region.
[01:50] Liam: If we start with PLG hosted and hit throughput limits, how seamless is the move to dedicated?
[01:55] Connor: It's designed to be friction-light — same API, you can pin a model version, and routing policy moves traffic to dedicated pool. you won't need to rewrite calls, just update routing config.
[02:09] Aria: Time-to-first-token — from signup to sending an authenticated request — what's realistic?
[02:14] Samir: For most teams it's under an hour: signup, SDK install, create API key, run quickstart example. with our free credits we provision a sandbox and a README that takes you to first token in 10–20 minutes if you follow steps.
[02:28] Maya: That sounds good. we want a reproducible runbook so our engineers can hand it off.
[02:34] Samir: We'll send a one-page quickstart + a recorded demo link.
[02:38] Raj: On data retention — if we use hosted for initial testing, can we disable retention and ensure logs are not stored?
[02:45] Elena: Yes, you can opt out of data retention per project; we also offer prefix caching policies so you can control KV cache. for pilot with dedicated we can enable full control and audit logs.
[02:58] Liam: Are there usage or token cost differences if we choose GPU-backed dedicated?
[03:02] Connor: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and usually lower unit cost at scale compared to pay-as-you-go hosted pricing, but there's a commitment. we can model costs given your expected qps and token distribution.
[03:15] Maya: Our immediate goal is to validate the product hypothesis — quality of responses on domain docs plus latency constraints — before committing to reserved capacity.
[03:24] Samir: Makes sense. typical approach: PLG/self-serve hosted for exploratory experiments using trial credits, then small dedicated pilot for latency and privacy needs. if you need private (VPC/on-prem) we can parallelize discussions with infra and security.
[03:38] Aria: How are rate limits applied? our alpha traffic will spike during internal testing.
[03:43] Elena: We set project-level quotas and token-based rate limits. for pilots we can bump limits and set burst capacity. and you can configure canary and fallback policies.
[03:55] Speaker 2: (interruption) do you support SSO for user access to console and team keys?
[03:58] Samir: Yes, SAML/SSO and granular RBAC. Enterprise accounts have admin controls and audit trails.
[04:05] Raj: For private deployment, what does the control plane look like? we need to know which API calls go over public internet.
[04:11] Connor: Private deployment keeps your control plane in your VPC; the control-plane traffic is via customer-managed networking. for air-gapped we have on-prem packaging too. we'll include a network diagram.
[04:24] Liam: Can you run performance tests against our docs? we want an apples-to-apples benchmark vs Anthropic/OpenAI.
[04:30] Elena: Yes we can help run a benchmark harness — we'll need a sample prompt set and a short dataset. for initial proof we can do hosted trials; for strict residency we can run them on dedicated or bring your own infra.
[04:42] Maya: What are typical success metrics for a pilot?
[04:45] Samir: Usually: quality pass rate on eval prompts (e.g., >=85% on domain QA), latency SLO (p95 < 1.2s for the target flow), and cost per succesful API call within expected budget. also time-to-first-token and onboarding friction are internal metrics.
[05:00] Aria: About prompt-engineering support — do you offer examples for retrieval-augmented generation?
[05:04] Elena: Yes, we have templates, embedding tooling, and recommendations for batching and cache TTLs. we also have quantization and model variant suggestions to optimize cost vs quality.
[05:16] Speaker 1: (inaudible) any gotchas moving from dev to production?
[05:19] Connor: Watch sequence length distribution, cold-start latency for KV cache, and make sure your prompt sets are covered by evals to catch quality regressions. Redwood Optimize can suggest batching and quantization changes.
[05:33] Maya: Security is the big blocker for us. if hosted is okay for experimentation, we need clear written answers on KMS, SSO, SOC2, and an SLA.
[05:42] Samir: Understood — Elena will attach the SOC2, network diagram, and KMS options. our SLAs are available for Dedicated customers; hosted has published uptime and incident processes.
[05:53] Aria: For trial credits — how long do they last and are they usable against embeddings and generation?
[05:58] Samir: Yes, trial credits are general purpose across API surfaces. typical trial lasts 30 days; we can adjust if you need a longer evaluation window for pilot coordination.
[06:07] Liam: If we do a pilot, we need to load-test with our traffic patterns — can Redwood support a spike test on reserved nodes?
[06:13] Elena: Absolutely. for dedicated pilots we provision reserved pools and simulate your qps to tune autoscaling and batching policies.
[06:22] Raj: Regarding data residency again — can you guarantee that logs are stored in our chosen region?
[06:27] Connor: For Dedicated and Private, yes. For hosted, we can provision regionally and disable retention per project, but absolute guarantees for hosted are in the enterprise contract.
[06:38] Aria: Any integrations with our existing observability? we use Datadog and internal tracing.
[06:43] Elena: We ship traces and per-route latency breakdowns; we can forward metrics to Datadog and provide token-level cost breakdowns.
[06:51] Speaker 2: (background) what about fallback policies if a model degrades?
[06:55] Samir: You can configure automated fallback to a compatible variant or a cheaper model; rollouts support canary and A/B.
[07:03] Maya: Let's talk timeline — we want to start experiments next week. is that realistic?
[07:07] Samir: Yes — I can provision trial credits today and send the quickstart. you'll likely hit first token in 10–60 minutes depending on approvals.
[07:16] Aria: Perfect. If we hit a blocker around PII, how quickly can you open a Dedicated pilot?
[07:21] Connor: Usually a couple of weeks to spin a small dedicated pool once contracts and infra details are agreed, sometimes faster with standard playbook.
[07:30] Liam: Who at Redwood will be our day-to-day contact during the trial?
[07:33] Samir: I'll be the primary AE, Elena and Connor will be the SEs. we'll create a Slack channel for the pilot.
[07:40] Speaker 1: (hiss) any pricing ballpark for a small dedicated footprint?
[07:44] Samir: We'll run a sizing exercise — ballpark for a small reserved GPU pool is in the low tens of thousands per month depending on model choice and throughput. I'll include an example spreadsheet.
[07:56] Maya: Ok, let's capture next steps.
[08:00] Samir: Recap: Samir to provision $5k trial credits and quickstart. Elena to send security pack (SOC2, KMS, network diagram). Connor to prepare options for a small dedicated pilot and a brief cost model. Maya to confirm pilot stakeholders and approval path. schedule a benchmark session week of 2026-09-08.
[08:20] Aria: Sounds good. any blockers?
[08:23] Raj: I'll need the SOC2 and details on KMS and audit logs before I sign off for pilot.
[08:29] Elena: We'll include those docs in the email.
[08:33] Samir: Great—thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and calendar invite.
[08:38] Maya: Thanks, appreciate it.
[45:30] (call ends; faint chatter)
